ratings.long_description: Specific and arguable; asserts common descent supported by converging evidence.
Somewhat vague, or states evolution without committing to common descent.
Missing, or just restates the prompt.
Three or more independent lines, each with a specific named example.
Three lines named but general, or fewer than three, or examples thin.
One line, or evidence described inaccurately.
Explains why each line supports common descent AND why convergence of independent lines is powerful; handles homologous vs. analogous.
Links evidence to the claim but with gaps; convergence or the homology distinction underdeveloped.
Lists evidence without explaining why it supports the claim.
Reads as one coherent argument and ties to variation (M5) and/or classification (M7); within the word range.
Components present but loosely connected.
Listed independently without connection.
Specific and arguable; asserts the molecularly based three-domain system over morphology alone.
Somewhat vague, or names three domains without committing to why.
Missing, or just restates the prompt.
Contrasts morphology vs. molecular (rRNA) evidence with a specific molecular difference cited.
Names both kinds of evidence but general, or one side thin.
One kind only, or evidence described inaccurately.
Explains why sequences record ancestry more reliably than appearance AND fairly weighs morphology’s value and limits.
Links evidence to the claim but with gaps; the “why molecules win” move underdeveloped.
States a preference without explaining why.
Reads as one coherent argument and ties to common descent (M6) and/or the molecules of M2/M5; within the word range.
Components present but loosely connected.
Listed independently without connection.
Specific and data-grounded; names the full pattern (rises with wind/heat/light, falls with humidity/dark).
States a direction but partial or vague about which factors do what.
Missing, or just restates the prompt.
Cites 3+ specific values, each compared to baseline.
Uses some data, but few numbers or no baseline comparison.
No data cited, or data misread.
Explains the mechanism for the conditions AND justifies cohesion-tension (pull + cohesion lifting the xylem column).
Links data to a cause but the cohesion-tension mechanism is thin or partly wrong.
Describes the data without explaining why.
Reads as one coherent argument and ties to water’s properties (M2) and/or the stomata–photosynthesis trade-off (M4); within the word range.
Components present but loosely connected.
Listed independently without connection.
Specific and defensible; names the drug and states what addiction to it fundamentally is.
States a position but vague about the drug or about addiction.
Missing, or just restates the prompt.
Synaptic action named correctly (neurotransmitter, receptor, mechanism) plus effect and repeated-use change.
Some correct biology, but a step is missing or a term misused.
Little accurate biology, or mechanism largely wrong.
Explains the full causal chain synapse → effect → neuroadaptation → tolerance/dependence.
Links mechanism to addiction but the neuroadaptation step is thin or partly wrong.
Describes the drug without explaining why addiction follows.
One coherent argument; ties addiction to homeostasis/self-government and reasons through the contested question; within word range.
Components present but the connection or the position is loose.
Listed independently; no position taken.
Specific and defensible; states what the combined evidence best supports.
States a position but vague or hedged into meaninglessness.
Missing, or just restates the prompt.
Three independent lines, cited concretely with real records/numbers.
Two lines, or three named only vaguely; some detail missing.
One line, or evidence largely inaccurate.
Explains mechanisms, argues why convergence is powerful, and fairly weighs a counter-consideration.
Links evidence to claim but convergence or counterpoint is thin.
Lists evidence without explaining why it supports the claim.
One coherent argument; reasons from the biology to a defensible stewardship position; within word range.
Components present but the position or connection is loose.
Listed independently; no position taken.
Three domains + kingdoms + plant station + key checkpoint, all labeled.
Most elements present and labeled.
Several elements missing or unlabeled.
Few elements present.
Organisms placed in correct domain/kingdom; plant tissues and transport modeled correctly.
Minor placement/tissue errors; core relationships correct.
Several errors in placement or transport.
Major conceptual errors.
Recording/snapshots show deliberate construction and revision.
Shows the construction process.
Limited process shown.
Final artifact only, no process.
Tour explains ordering and structure→function clearly.
Mostly clear explanation.
Partial or unclear explanation.
Little or no explanation.
Pyramid, cycle, homeostasis, and stewardship stations + capstone marker, all labeled.
Most stations present and labeled.
Several elements missing or unlabeled.
Few elements present.
Trophic levels and 10% energy loss correct; cycle flows accurate; homeostasis station shows a valid feedback loop.
Minor errors; core flows and loop correct.
Several errors in flows or feedback logic.
Major conceptual errors.
Recording/snapshots show deliberate construction and revision.
Shows the construction process.
Limited process shown.
Final artifact only, no process.

# Week 36 Final — Quiz Specification (Bank-Draw Logic + Counts)

**Biology 1 (Florida 2000310) · Semester 2 Final · Modules 1–10 cumulative (full year)**
**Format: 70 multiple-choice (EOC-format) + 3 CER short-response · EOC-aligned**

This file specifies **how the final is assembled from the existing full-year reading-quiz bank** — it is not itself a set of new questions. Build the exam in Canvas as a native Quiz. Do **not** generate Canvas XML. Every MC item already exists, vetted and answer-keyed, in the 34 weekly `reading-quiz.md` files; the final *draws* from them. The 3 CER items are teacher-scored short responses, specified in full at the end.

The final follows the same method as the Week-15 Midterm, extended to the whole year: a stratified draw from the accumulated bank, weighted by module size, balanced against the EOC domain weights, with high-value misconception anchors guaranteed a seat.

---

## 1. The full-year bank it draws from

Every reading-quiz item was written to stand alone as a reusable bank item and to be EOC-format, so any of them can appear on the final unmodified (CLAUDE.md hard rule). The full-year bank is the union of all Module 1–10 weekly quizzes:

| Module | Title | Weeks | Items/wk | Module pool | Source files |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Nature of Science | 1–2 | 8 | **16** | `module-01-nature-of-science/week-0{1,2}/reading-quiz.md` |
| 2 | Chemistry of Life | 3–4 | 8 | **16** | `module-02-chemistry-of-life/week-0{3,4}/reading-quiz.md` |
| 3 | Cell Structure, Function & Transport | 5–7 | 9 | **27** | `module-03-cell-structure-function-transport/week-0{5,6,7}/reading-quiz.md` |
| 4 | Cell Energy | 8–10 | 9 | **27** | `module-04-cell-energy/week-{08,09,10}/reading-quiz.md` |
| 5 | DNA, Cell Division & Genetics | 11–14 | 10 | **40** | `module-05-dna-cell-division-genetics/week-{11,12,13,14}/reading-quiz.md` |
| 6 | Evolution and Natural Selection | 16–18 | 9 | **27** | `module-06-evolution-and-natural-selection/week-{16,17,18}/reading-quiz.md` |
| 7 | Classification and Diversity of Life | 19–22 | 10 | **40** | `module-07-classification-and-diversity-of-life/week-{19,20,21,22}/reading-quiz.md` |
| 8 | Plant Biology | 23–25 | 9 | **27** | `module-08-plant-biology/week-{23,24,25}/reading-quiz.md` |
| 9 | Human Body Systems | 26–29 | 10 | **40** | `module-09-human-body-systems/week-{26,27,28,29}/reading-quiz.md` |

| | | **34 wk** | | **314 total** | |

The final pulls **70** of these 314 for the MC section.

---

## 2. MC draw — counts by module (nudged from proportional to module size toward EOC domain weights)

70 MC allocated across all ten modules per `plan.md` §7. The split is nudged from a pure size-proportional split (70/34 weeks = M1 4.1, M2 4.1, M3 6.2, M4 6.2, M5 8.2, M6 6.2, M7 8.2, M8 6.2, M9 8.2, M10 12.4). Deviations: M1 3 (-1.1), M2 5 (+0.9), M6 8 (+1.8), M7 7 (-1.2), M8 5 (-1.2), M9 10 (+1.8), M10 12 (-0.4); M3, M4, M5 are within 0.2 of proportional. The aim is to approach the EOC domain weights (Molecular/Cellular 35–40%, Classification/Evolution 20–25%, Ecosystems/Ecology 20–25%, Human Anatomy/Physiology 15–20%).

| Module | Weeks | **MC drawn** | EOC domain |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 — Nature of Science | 2 | **3** | Nature of Science (woven through all) |
| 2 — Chemistry of Life | 2 | **5** | Molecular/Cellular |
| 3 — Cell Structure & Transport | 3 | **6** | Molecular/Cellular |
| 4 — Cell Energy | 3 | **6** | Molecular/Cellular |
| 5 — DNA, Division & Genetics | 4 | **8** | Molecular/Cellular |
| 6 — Evolution | 3 | **8** | Classification/Evolution |
| 7 — Classification & Diversity | 4 | **7** | Classification/Evolution |
| 8 — Plant Biology | 3 | **5** | Organismal (plants) |
| 9 — Human Body Systems | 4 | **10** | Human Anatomy/Physiology |
| 10 — Ecology | 6 | **12** | Ecosystems/Ecology |
| **Total** | **34** | **70** | — |

**Resulting domain shares:** Molecular/Cellular (M2–M5) = 25/70 ≈ **36%** · Classification/Evolution (M6–M7) = 15/70 ≈ **21%** · Ecology (M10) = 12/70 ≈ **17%** · Human Anatomy (M9) = 10/70 ≈ **14%** · plants (M8) ≈ 7% and Nature of Science (M1) ≈ 4% make up the balance (NOS is also woven through every domain item). These match the `plan.md` §7 targets. Molecular/Cellular (36%) and Classification/Evolution (21%) sit inside their EOC bands; Ecology (17% vs. 20–25%) and Human Anatomy (14% vs. 15–20%) sit slightly below theirs, because module size and the plants/NOS balance share the remaining weight. Molecular/cellular carries the largest share, as on the EOC.

> **Optional rebalance (per `plan.md` §7 open decision):** to push ecology toward the top of its EOC band (~20%), move 2 items from M9→M10 (M9: 8, M10: 14). Keep the total at 70. Note this lifts ecology to 20% but drops anatomy to 11%, further below its band; it is an optional alternative, not a fix. The build below uses the table above; apply the rebalance only if instructed.

### 2a. Sub-allocation by week (keeps coverage even within a module)

| Module | Per-week draw | Sums to |

| 1 | Wk 1: 2 · Wk 2: 1 | 3 |
| 2 | Wk 3: 3 · Wk 4: 2 | 5 |
| 3 | Wk 5: 2 · Wk 6: 2 · Wk 7: 2 | 6 |

---

## 3. Required-coverage rule (the draw is *stratified*, not blind-random)

The per-week counts above set the quotas. Within each week, selection is random **except** that the following high-value, EOC-targeted **misconception anchors must be guaranteed a seat** (each is a documented misconception from `eoc_review.md`). Fill the remaining seats randomly from that week's pool. This ensures the exam tests the misconceptions the course was built to correct, not an accidental easy subset.

**Must-include anchors (one item each, drawn from the named module):**

- **M1** — theory vs. law (a theory is *not* "a guess that grew up"); identifying the controlled variable / control group in a described experiment.
- **M2** — water's specific heat / hydrogen bonding explains cohesion, ice, solvent behavior; a protein's *function follows its folded shape* (denaturation).
- **M3** — osmosis is the movement of *water* (direction by solute concentration); RBC in hypo-/hyper-/isotonic solution; active transport requires energy (Na⁺/K⁺ pump).
- **M4** — photosynthesis and respiration are *not* simple reverses; the Calvin cycle does not require *direct* light; O₂ is the *final electron acceptor*; energy flows, matter cycles.
- **M5** — transcription vs. translation (where each occurs); meiosis produces genetically unique cells; "dominant" ≠ "more common"; a single base substitution → amino-acid change → protein → phenotype (sickle cell).
- **M6** — *fitness* means reproductive success, not "strongest"; natural selection acts on *existing* variation (it does not create traits on demand); acquired traits are not inherited; antibiotic resistance as evolution in real time.
- **M7** — the three domains rest on *molecular* data, not body shape; a cladogram groups by *shared derived characters*; classification reflects evolutionary history (common descent).
- **M8** — water rises in xylem by *cohesion-tension* driven by transpiration (not "pumped up" by the roots); stomata/guard cells control water loss; plants sense and respond (tropisms) without nerves.
- **M9** — homeostasis works by *negative* feedback; the neuron uses the Na⁺/K⁺ pump (callback to M3); a vaccine does not cause the disease; antibody specificity is a shape→function case.
- **M10** — energy *flows* (one way) while matter *cycles*; the 10% rule limits trophic levels; carbon links photosynthesis/respiration to the atmosphere; evidence for anthropogenic climate change comes from *independent* lines.

> If a future re-build adds more items to a week's pool, keep the per-week quotas in §2a and re-run the stratified draw; the anchors above stay mandatory. Because the final is cumulative, an item already used on the Week-15 Midterm **may** reappear here (the midterm and final are separate administrations); if you prefer no overlap, exclude the 50 midterm items from the M1–M5 sub-pools before drawing.

---

## 4. Assembly rules (Canvas)

1. **No duplication within the exam.** Each of the 70 MC is a distinct bank item; none repeats within the final.
2. **Preserve the vetted item verbatim.** Use each item's stem, four options, flagged correct answer, and (optionally) its explanation as Canvas answer feedback. Distractors are already misconception-based — do not edit.
3. **Shuffle.** Shuffle question order and answer-option order at delivery (Canvas Quiz settings). Because every item stands alone, shuffling is safe.
4. **One point per MC** = 70 points for the MC section.
5. **Group by Canvas Question Banks.** Recommended: maintain ten Canvas Question Banks (one per module) populated from the weekly `reading-quiz.md` items, then use a Quiz with ten question groups set to pull the §2 counts. Pin the §3 anchor items as fixed questions (outside the random groups) so they always appear, and reduce that group's random pull by the number pinned. (This extends the five-bank setup already built for the midterm to all ten modules.)
6. **EOC format throughout** — single-best-answer MC, plain stems, no "all of the above," targeting the documented misconceptions.

---

## 5. CER short-response section (3 items, teacher-scored)

Three analytical short-response CER items, one from each of the year's three great domains (`plan.md` §7, `cer_guide.md`). These are **shorter than the ~400–700-word module essays** — each is a focused ~150–250-word claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph written during the exam. They are **teacher-reviewed, not auto-graded.**

The three sample the full spine: **molecular** (energy & matter), **genetic/evolutionary** (information → variation → common descent), and **ecological** (the living planet).

### CER 1 — Molecular (Modules 4 + 10 anchor; the carbon-atom trace)

> Follow a single **carbon atom** as it enters a plant, becomes part of a sugar, and is later released again. Start with a CO₂ molecule in the air. Trace the atom through **photosynthesis** (into glucose) and then through **cellular respiration** (back to CO₂), naming where each stage happens and what happens to the carbon. Write a claim, cite the steps as evidence, and explain the *mechanism* — including why "energy flows one way but matter cycles" is true for this atom.

*Targets the Module 4 CER focus (photosynthesis/respiration as complementary, not reverse, processes) and the Module 10 carbon-cycle connection. Rewards the M4↔M10 bridge from the review lesson.*

### CER 2 — Genetic / Evolutionary (Modules 5 + 6 anchor; mutation → variation → common descent)

> Explain how a change in **DNA** can, over many generations, become evidence that two species share a **common ancestor**. Begin with a single mutation in one organism. Write a claim, then use as evidence the chain: mutation → heritable variation (via meiosis/reproduction) → natural selection acting on that variation → accumulated differences → the molecular and anatomical similarities we later read as common descent. Explain the *mechanism* at each step — especially why variation must be *heritable* to matter, and why shared DNA sequences are strong evidence of shared ancestry.

*Targets the Module 5→Module 6 bridge (heritable variation is the raw material of selection) and the Module 6 CER focus (independent lines of evidence for common descent). Rewards the M5→M6 bridge from the review lesson.*

### CER 3 — Ecological *(primary form: climate evidence; alternate form: energy flow)*

**Form A (primary) — Evidence for climate change (Module 10 anchor):**

> Scientists argue that recent climate change is driven by human activity. Identify **three independent lines of evidence** that support this claim (for example: the instrumental temperature record, rising atmospheric CO₂ with its isotopic "fingerprint," and shifts in species' ranges or timing). Write a claim, present the three lines as evidence, and explain the *reasoning* — why *independent* lines converging on the same conclusion make the argument strong, the same way independent lines made the case for evolution.

*Targets the Module 10 CER focus (evaluate anthropogenic climate change from three independent sources) and reuses the Module 6 reasoning about convergent independent evidence.*

**Form B (alternate) — Energy flow & the 10% rule (Module 10 anchor):**

> A food chain runs: grass → grasshopper → mouse → hawk. Explain why there are far fewer hawks than blades of grass. Write a claim, use the 10% rule and the idea of trophic levels as evidence, and explain the *mechanism* — where the "lost" 90% of the energy goes at each step, and why this means "energy flows but matter cycles." Connect it back to where the energy first entered the chain (plant photosynthesis).

*Targets the Module 10 energy-flow focus and the M8→M10 and M4→M10 bridges. Use Form B if Form A overlaps too heavily with recent work, or alternate forms across sections.*

### CER scoring — 6 points each (18 points total)

Each CER is scored on the same three components as the year's CER framework, compressed for a timed short-response and weighting reasoning (the mechanism) most heavily — identical to the midterm rubric:

| Component | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | Max |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Claim** | No/incorrect claim | A clear, correct, specific claim that answers the prompt | — | — | **1** |
| **Evidence** | None/irrelevant | Some correct evidence, with gaps | Accurate, specific evidence naming the relevant steps/facts | — | **2** |
| **Reasoning (mechanism)** | None | States *what* happens but not *why* | Explains the mechanism with one or more gaps | Explains *why* each step forces the next; mechanism complete | **3** |
| | | | | **Per CER** | **6** |

**CER section = 3 × 6 = 18 points.**

---

## 6. Scoring summary

| Section | Items | Points | Scored |
|---|---|---|---|
| Multiple choice | 70 | 70 (1 each) | Auto-graded (Canvas) |
| CER short-response | 3 | 18 (6 each) | Teacher-reviewed |
| **Final total** | **73 prompts** | **88 raw** | scale to 100% |

> Weighting note: the final counts toward the **Midterm & Final** grading category (10%), per the syllabus. The MC section is auto-graded, so the only teacher-review load is the 3 CER short-responses (≈2 minutes each), consistent with the course's 500:1 design target.

---

## 7. Sources & alignment (builder reference — never student-facing)

- **Bank source:** the 34 full-year `reading-quiz.md` files listed in §1 (314 vetted EOC items).
- **Draw counts:** `plan.md` §7 (final bank-draw table and EOC domain-weight targets).
- **Misconception anchors:** `01_Analysis/eoc_review.md` (per-unit common misconceptions).
- **CER prompts & rubric:** `plan.md` §7 (three final CER domains) and `01_Analysis/cer_guide.md` (3-component CER framework).
- **Cross-unit reasoning:** `plan.md` §8 spine bridges — the CER prompts deliberately reward the M4↔M10, M5→M6, and M8/M4→M10 connections traced in the Week-36 review lesson.
- **Hard rules honored:** no NGSSS codes and no OpenStax references appear on the student-facing exam; every MC could appear on the EOC unmodified.

quizzes.title: Week 1 Reading Quiz: Evidence for evolution

questions.text: A geologist studies a cliff with four undisturbed rock layers. Which statement is correct about the relative ages of the layers?

answers.text: The top layer is the oldest because it has been exposed to the surface the longest
All four layers are the same age because they belong to the same cliff face
The bottom layer is the oldest because deeper layers were deposited first
The middle layers are the oldest because they are the most protected from erosion

questions.text: What makes a species useful as an index fossil for dating rock layers?

answers.text: It was geographically widespread but existed for only a short span of time
It survived almost unchanged for hundreds of millions of years across many habitats
It was very large and left big fossils that are easy for collectors to find
It is still alive today, so scientists can compare it directly with living members

questions.text: Tiktaalik, about 375 million years old, had fish scales and gills but also a flat head, a neck, and sturdy fin bones with wrist-like joints. What does such a transitional fossil best demonstrate?

answers.text: That fish alive today are slowly turning into land animals over time
That all fossils are transitional forms between two living groups
That fish and land animals have no evolutionary relationship at all
That an ancient form can bridge two major groups and document change

questions.text: A human arm, a whale flipper, and a bat wing all contain the same bones in the same arrangement, even though they are used for grasping, swimming, and flying. These are best described as:

answers.text: Analogous structures, because they perform different jobs
Homologous structures, which point to a common ancestor
Vestigial structures, because they are leftovers from earlier forms
Identical structures, which carry no evolutionary meaning at all

questions.text: A bird's wing and an insect's wing both produce flight but are built from completely different structures. A student concludes that birds and insects must be closely related. Why is this reasoning flawed?

answers.text: Shared function can evolve independently, so analogous structures do not prove close relationship
Birds and insects are in fact the same kind of animal, so their wings must have identical bones
Insects do not really fly the way birds do, so the comparison itself is invalid
Only structures used for movement count as evidence of relationship in biology

questions.text: On a remote island far from any continent, biologists find lizard species that exist nowhere else on Earth, yet most closely resemble lizards of the nearest mainland. Under common descent, why is this the expected pattern?

answers.text: Because the island and the mainland happen to share nearly identical climates and habitats
Because lizards can only survive in warm tropical regions close to the equator on any continent
Because island species were created separately and only look similar by coincidence
Because a few mainland ancestors reached the island and their descendants changed in isolation

questions.text: Which statement accurately describes how the theory of evolution by natural selection came to be published?

answers.text: Darwin published immediately after his Beagle voyage, and no other naturalist reached the idea
Darwin delayed publishing; Wallace independently reached the same idea, and their work was presented jointly in 1858
Wallace published first in 1859, and Darwin rejected the idea of natural selection
Darwin and Wallace were the same person, publishing under two different names at two different times

questions.text: Human and chimpanzee DNA are extremely similar. What does this similarity actually indicate?

answers.text: Humans evolved directly from modern chimpanzees over millions of years
Humans and chimpanzees are unrelated species with similar DNA by coincidence
Humans and chimpanzees share a relatively recent common ancestor
Chimpanzees will eventually evolve into humans given enough time

questions.text: Why do scientists consider the case for common descent especially strong?

answers.text: Because independent lines of evidence (fossils, anatomy, biogeography, molecules) all converge
Because a single exceptionally complete fossil proves it beyond any doubt
Because evolution is aimed at producing better and more advanced organisms over time
Because all scientists simply agree to accept it without ever testing it against new data

quizzes.title: Week 2 Reading Quiz: Natural selection & other mechanisms

questions.text: Which set of conditions must be present for natural selection to occur in a population?

answers.text: Identical individuals, no inheritance, and unlimited resources available for every offspring that is born
Large body size, great physical strength, and a long lifespan in each individual
A goal the species is working toward and an environment that never changes at all
Heritable variation, overproduction of offspring, and differential reproductive success

questions.text: In biology, what does it mean to say one organism has higher "fitness" than another?

answers.text: It leaves more surviving, reproducing offspring in its environment
It can run faster or fight better than competitors in its habitat
It is physically stronger and larger than other members of its group
It lives the longest, whether or not it ever reproduces

questions.text: A population of beetles lives on dark soil. The beetles range from pale tan to dark brown, color is inherited, and birds hunt them by sight. After many generations, which prediction is correct?

answers.text: Each individual beetle gradually turns dark brown to hide from the hunting birds
The beetles sense the danger and decide to become darker to avoid being eaten
The population becomes mostly dark brown because dark beetles reproduce more
Nothing changes, because beetle color cannot affect survival or reproduction at all

questions.text: As soot from industry darkened tree bark in Britain, dark peppered moths became far more common than light ones, then declined again after clean-air laws reduced the soot. This is an example of which type of selection?

answers.text: Stabilizing selection, which favors the average form of the trait
Directional selection, which pushes the trait toward one extreme
Disruptive selection, which favors both extremes over the middle
Artificial selection, which relies on humans choosing who breeds

questions.text: In a bird population, both small-beaked and large-beaked birds survive and reproduce well, but medium-beaked birds do poorly because only small soft seeds and large hard seeds are available. Which type of selection is this?

answers.text: Stabilizing selection, because the average form is preserved in the population
Directional selection, because the population shifts toward one extreme
Disruptive selection, because both extremes are favored over the middle
Genetic drift, because the change is random and unrelated to fitness

questions.text: Modern corn was bred over thousands of years from a wild grass called teosinte, and all dog breeds descend from wolves. How does this artificial selection compare with natural selection?

answers.text: It uses the same mechanism, but humans rather than the environment choose who breeds
It works through a completely different mechanism than natural selection uses
It does not involve heredity at all, since breeders only change the environment
It shows that organisms can change their own traits on purpose within one lifetime

questions.text: A disease sweeps through a large population of lizards, killing all but a dozen survivors whose allele frequencies do not match the original population. The survivors rebuild the population. This is an example of:

answers.text: The founder effect, in which a few individuals start a new population
Directional selection, in which one extreme of a trait is favored
Gene flow, in which individuals migrate between populations
The bottleneck effect, in which a sudden crash leaves few survivors

questions.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes the mechanisms of evolution?

answers.text: Genetic drift occurs only in very large populations, where chance matters most
Genetic drift is random change in allele frequencies, but selection is non-random
Gene flow between populations makes them more different from each other
Mutation can only remove existing alleles and can never create new ones

questions.text: A bacterial population is exposed to an antibiotic and becomes resistant over several generations. Which explanation is correct?

answers.text: A few cells were already resistant by random mutation, and they survived and reproduced
The bacteria gradually tried harder to become resistant until they finally succeeded in surviving
The antibiotic triggered new resistance mutations in each cell it touched
The antibiotic taught the bacteria how to survive its own effects

quizzes.title: Week 3 Reading Quiz: Speciation & origins

questions.text: Two populations of birds are separated by a tall mountain range. Over many generations they develop different mating calls and can no longer interbreed. This is an example of which type of speciation?

answers.text: Sympatric speciation, because both populations remained in the same location
Allopatric speciation, because a geographic barrier separated the populations
Genetic drift only, because the mountains changed allele frequencies by chance
Convergent evolution, because both groups independently evolved similar traits

questions.text: By the biological species concept, what makes two populations members of the same species?

answers.text: They look very much alike in size, shape, and coloring
They currently live in the same geographic area
They eat the same kinds of food in the same habitat
They can interbreed in nature and produce fertile offspring

questions.text: Why is reproductive isolation necessary for one species to split into two?

answers.text: It stops gene flow, so the separated populations can diverge independently
It makes the two populations look more different from each other at once
It increases the number of offspring each population produces each year
It prevents mutations from occurring in either of the separated populations

questions.text: A population is in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium. What does this tell you about that population?

answers.text: It has stopped reproducing, so no new alleles can enter the population
It is evolving very rapidly, so allele frequencies shift each generation
Its allele frequencies are not changing, so it is not evolving
All of its members are genetically identical, so there is no variation

questions.text: Which of the following would cause a population to depart from Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium?

answers.text: Random mating among all of the individuals in the population
A very large population size, so that chance has little effect
No migration into or out of the population during the generations
Natural selection favoring one genotype over the others in each generation

questions.text: The Miller–Urey experiment (1953) sparked a mixture of simple gases and produced amino acids. What did this experiment demonstrate?

answers.text: That organic building blocks of life can form from simple gases and energy
That a living cell can be created from simple gases and an energy source
That life on Earth must have first arrived from outer space on meteorites
That spontaneous generation of living organisms is true in everyday settings

questions.text: A student says, "Since Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation, science has also answered how the first life on Earth originated." Why is this reasoning flawed?

answers.text: Pasteur's experiment actually proved that spontaneous generation occurs in everyday life
They are different questions: Pasteur tested everyday spontaneous generation, not how life first arose
Pasteur's experiment was never accepted, so spontaneous generation is still believed
The origin of life has been fully explained and is no longer studied by scientists

questions.text: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between humans and chimpanzees?

answers.text: Humans evolved directly from the modern chimpanzees we see today over millions of years
Chimpanzees are slowly evolving into humans and will eventually reach that form
Humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor from roughly 6–7 million years ago
Humans and chimpanzees are unrelated species that only look somewhat similar

questions.text: Which statement about human evolution is accurate?

answers.text: Human evolution was a branching bush of many related species, most now extinct
Human evolution was a straight ladder of species leading directly to modern humans
Only one human-like species existed at a time, each replacing the one before
Evolution has a built-in goal of producing ever more intelligent species over time

quizzes.title: Week 4 Reading Quiz: Taxonomy & nomenclature

questions.text: Which list places the levels of classification in the correct order, from broadest to most specific?

answers.text: Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum, Kingdom, Domain
Kingdom, Domain, Phylum, Order, Class, Family, Species, Genus
Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Domain, Phylum, Kingdom, Class, Family, Order, Genus, Species

questions.text: Which statement correctly compares two levels of the hierarchy?

answers.text: A species is the most specific level, with members sharing the most traits
A genus contains more different kinds of organisms than a phylum, since it ranks higher
A kingdom is a more specific level than a species, so its members share more traits
A domain contains the fewest organisms of any level, since it is the most exclusive group

questions.text: Two organisms are classified in the same family but different genera. A third pair is classified only in the same kingdom. What can you conclude?

answers.text: The kingdom-only pair is more closely related, because a broad group means more in common
Relationship cannot be judged from classification, because ranks are only labels
Both pairs are equally related, because all of them share the same kingdom
The family pair is more closely related, because a narrower level means more shared traits

questions.text: Which of the following is the correctly written scientific name for the gray wolf?

answers.text: canis lupus
Canis lupus
Canis Lupus
canis Lupus

questions.text: In the scientific name Panthera leo (the lion), what do the two parts represent?

answers.text: The genus (Panthera) and the specific epithet (leo)
The kingdom (Panthera) and the phylum (leo)
The common name (Panthera) and the Latin name (leo)
The order (Panthera) and the family (leo)

questions.text: A student says, "Common names work fine, so scientific names are unnecessary." Which fact best shows why scientific names are needed?

answers.text: Common names are always shorter and easier for scientists to remember
Every organism has exactly one common name used worldwide
Scientific names are used only for animals, never for plants
The same common name, such as "robin," can refer to different species

questions.text: What is a dichotomous key used for, and how is it structured?

answers.text: It ranks organisms from most to least advanced using a single trait
It lists every known species in alphabetical order by common name
It identifies an organism through a series of paired, either/or choices
It measures how closely related two organisms are by comparing their DNA

questions.text: A short key reads: 1a. Wings present → go to 2; 1b. Wings absent → go to 3; 2a. One pair of wings → Housefly; 2b. Two pairs of wings → Butterfly. An unknown insect has wings, in two pairs. Which path and identification are correct?

They are converted into urea so that the body can dispose of them

questions.text: A resting neuron's negative resting potential depends on steep Na⁺ and K⁺ gradients across its membrane. What maintains those gradients?

answers.text: Myelin, which physically blocks every ion from crossing the neuron's membrane
The dendrites, which soak up extra positive charge arriving from other cells
The sodium–potassium pump, using ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ in
Passive diffusion alone, which moves each ion down its gradient without energy

questions.text: A neuron receives a much stronger stimulus than usual (well above threshold). How does this change the action potentials it fires?

answers.text: The action potentials stay the same size, but the neuron fires them more often
Each action potential becomes larger and taller as the stimulus gets stronger
The neuron fires a single giant action potential and then cannot fire again
The action potentials become smaller and fewer to protect the cell from damage

questions.text: When an action potential reaches the end of one neuron's axon, how does the signal cross the synapse to the next cell?

answers.text: The electrical current leaps directly across the gap between the cells like a spark
The two neurons touch each other at the synapse, so the charge flows straight through
Neurotransmitters are released, cross the gap, and bind receptors on the next cell
The myelin sheath carries the electrical current across the cleft to the next cell

questions.text: Caffeine binds adenosine receptors but does not activate them, blocking the neurotransmitter adenosine (which normally causes drowsiness) from acting. Caffeine is therefore acting as a(n):

answers.text: Agonist — it mimics the neurotransmitter and activates the receptor
Reuptake inhibitor — it keeps adenosine in the cleft for longer
Enzyme — it breaks the adenosine apart before it can act
Antagonist — it blocks the receptor without turning it on

questions.text: Many different addictive drugs converge on the same result in the brain, and repeated use leads to tolerance. Which statement is correct?

answers.text: They flood the dopamine reward pathway, and the brain adapts by reducing its receptors
They destroy all of the brain's neurons permanently, even after a single use
They lower dopamine below its normal level, which is why the drug feels rewarding
The brain adds extra receptors, so each repeated dose feels stronger over time

questions.text: A hormone is released into the bloodstream and travels to every part of the body, yet it affects only certain cells. Why?

answers.text: The hormone runs out of energy before it reaches most of the cells
Only the target cells carry the matching receptor that the hormone binds to
The hormone is too large to leave the blood vessels near most other cells
Blood flows only to the cells that the hormone is meant to affect

questions.text: Blood glucose rises after a meal. Which gland and hormone bring it back down, and how?

answers.text: The thyroid releases glucagon, which signals the liver to release stored glucose
The adrenal glands release cortisol, which signals the brain to store extra glucose
The pituitary releases ADH, which signals the kidneys to remove glucose in urine
The pancreas releases insulin, which signals cells to take glucose in and store it

questions.text: Which statement best compares the nervous and endocrine systems?

answers.text: Both systems send electrical signals through the blood at about the same speed
The endocrine system is faster because hormones travel at the speed of electricity
Nervous signals are fast and brief; endocrine signals are slower and longer-lasting
Nervous signals are slow and last for days; endocrine signals are fast and brief

quizzes.title: Week 14 Reading Quiz: Defense & integration

questions.text: Which set of words best describes the innate immune system?

answers.text: Slow, specific, and with memory
Fast, general, and with no memory
Fast, specific, and with lifelong memory
Slow, general, and with some memory

questions.text: Skin, mucus, cilia, and stomach acid are all examples of:

answers.text: The second line of defense, which attacks microbes inside the body
Antibodies made by B cells in response to an earlier infection
The first line of defense, barriers that keep invaders out of the body
Memory cells that remain after an earlier infection has cleared

questions.text: During inflammation at a cut, a white blood cell engulfs and digests bacteria without identifying exactly which species they are. This cell is a:

answers.text: Phagocyte, an innate cell that acts on invaders in general
B cell, an adaptive cell that makes specific antibodies
Memory T cell, an adaptive cell that recalls past infections
Red blood cell, a cell that carries oxygen to the tissues

questions.text: What is the role of a B cell in adaptive immunity?

answers.text: It raises body temperature to produce a fever
It engulfs and digests any microbe that it happens to meet
It forms a physical barrier on the skin's surface
It produces antibodies that bind a specific antigen

questions.text: An antibody binds to only one specific antigen, "like a lock fits one key." This specificity comes from the antibody's:

answers.text: Electric charge, which repels all other molecules
Speed of movement, which lets it reach the antigen first
Folded three-dimensional shape, which matches the antigen
Ability to copy the antigen's DNA, which marks it for removal

questions.text: Which correctly pairs each T cell with its job?

answers.text: Helper T cells destroy infected cells; cytotoxic T cells coordinate the response
Helper T cells coordinate the response; cytotoxic T cells destroy infected cells
Helper T cells produce antibodies; cytotoxic T cells engulf microbes whole
Helper T cells form skin barriers; cytotoxic T cells form mucous barriers

questions.text: Years after recovering from an illness, a person is still immune to it. What is chiefly responsible for this lasting protection?

answers.text: Antibodies that stay in the blood at high levels for the rest of life
The innate system, which learns to recognize that microbe
A permanent change to the person's DNA that records the microbe
Long-lived memory B cells and memory T cells that persist for years

questions.text: In clonal selection, which lymphocyte multiplies into an army of identical cells during an infection?

answers.text: The one lymphocyte whose receptor matches the invader's antigen
Every lymphocyte in the body, all multiplying at the same time
Only the red blood cells that are located near the site of infection
Whichever lymphocyte happens to be closest to the wound or cut

questions.text: Why can a vaccine not give you the disease it protects against?

answers.text: It contains a full-strength pathogen that replicates freely, but the immune system destroys it before any symptoms can appear
It permanently rewrites the DNA in the person's cells so that the immune system is no longer needed, which blocks the disease from ever developing
It has either no pathogen able to replicate (inactivated, subunit, mRNA) or one weakened to replicate only slightly and cause no disease in healthy people
It replaces the person's natural immune system with a stronger artificial one that destroys any pathogen before illness can start

questions.text: Gametes (sperm and eggs) are produced by meiosis so that each carries half a chromosome set. This matters because:

answers.text: It allows a single parent to produce offspring that are identical clones of itself
Fertilization then restores the full chromosome number and combines two parents' genes
It removes the need for hormones from the endocrine system to coordinate reproduction
Half a chromosome set is all that a complete human being needs to develop

quizzes.title: Week 15 Reading Quiz: Levels, interactions, biomes

questions.text: A student writes, "A bird's habitat and its niche are two words for the same thing." Why is this incorrect?

answers.text: Habitat and niche both describe only what an animal eats, since feeding is the main way a species is defined
Habitat is the organism's full role and way of life, while niche is simply the physical place where it lives
Only plants have a habitat, because they stay in one place, while only animals have a niche, because they move around
Habitat is the place where the organism lives, while niche is its full role: what it eats, when it is active, and how it interacts

questions.text: Which sequence lists the ecological levels of organization correctly from smallest to largest?

answers.text: Organism → population → community → ecosystem → biome → biosphere
Organism → community → population → biome → ecosystem → biosphere
Population → organism → ecosystem → community → biosphere → biome
Biosphere → biome → ecosystem → community → population → organism

questions.text: Which list contains only abiotic factors of a pond ecosystem?

answers.text: Fish, algae, water temperature, and sunlight
Sunlight, water temperature, salinity, and pH
A decaying leaf, sunlight, pH, and a frog
Dissolved oxygen, bacteria, and a lily pad

questions.text: Inside coral tissue, algae called zooxanthellae make sugars the coral uses, and the coral gives the algae shelter. Both partners benefit. What is this relationship?

answers.text: Commensalism (+ / 0)
Parasitism (+ / −)
Mutualism (+ / +)
Predation (+ / −)

questions.text: A barnacle attaches to a whale's skin and is carried to richer feeding waters, while the whale is essentially unaffected. This is best classified as:

answers.text: Commensalism, because one benefits and the other is unaffected
Parasitism, because the barnacle lives on the whale and feeds there
Mutualism, because the two organisms live together in close contact
Competition, because they share the same ocean habitat

questions.text: Two hawks hunt the same field of mice, and neither can catch as many as it would alone. Which interaction is this, and what is its effect on the two hawks?

answers.text: Predation; one hawk is helped and the other is harmed
Mutualism; both hawks are helped by sharing the field (+ / +)
Commensalism; one hawk is helped and the other unaffected
Competition; both hawks lose out on the shared prey (− / −)

questions.text: In Florida's longleaf pine savanna, the gopher tortoise digs long burrows that shelter hundreds of other animal species. Because its impact on the community is far greater than its numbers, the gopher tortoise is best described as:

answers.text: A primary producer that captures energy for the community
A keystone species with outsized effects on its community
A parasite that feeds on the pine trees' tissues
An abiotic factor that shapes the soil and habitat

questions.text: An ecologist can often identify a biome knowing only two measurements about a place. Which two?

answers.text: Its latitude and its elevation above sea level
Its soil color and its average daily wind speed
Its average temperature and its annual precipitation
Its number of animal species and plant species

questions.text: A climatograph shows a temperature line that stays high and nearly flat all year and precipitation bars that are tall in every month. Which biome does it describe?

answers.text: Subtropical desert
Treeless arctic tundra
Cold northern taiga
Tropical rainforest

quizzes.title: Week 16 Reading Quiz: Energy flow

questions.text: Which statement correctly describes how energy and matter move through an ecosystem?

answers.text: Both energy and matter are recycled through the ecosystem and used over and over again
Energy flows one way and is ultimately lost as heat, while matter cycles and is reused
Energy is recycled by decomposers, while matter flows one way and is lost as heat
Energy and matter both flow one way through the ecosystem and are lost as heat

questions.text: The producers in a field store 20,000 units of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much energy is available to the secondary consumers (the third trophic level)?

answers.text: 20,000 units
18,000 units
2,000 units
200 units

questions.text: Why do most food chains have only four or five links, with very few top predators?

answers.text: About 90% of the energy is lost at each step, so too little remains to support more levels
Predators choose not to hunt beyond the fourth level because larger prey are too dangerous
There are not enough kinds of animals in most ecosystems to build chains any longer
Energy increases at each higher level, so the top becomes crowded with too many predators

questions.text: In a forest, a mushroom growing on a dead log breaks the log down into simple nutrients that return to the soil. What role is the mushroom playing?

answers.text: Producer, because it makes its own food from sunlight using chlorophyll
Primary consumer, because it feeds on living plants and grasses
Decomposer, because it breaks down dead material and recycles matter
Secondary consumer, because it eats primary consumers for energy

questions.text: Why is a food web generally more stable than a single food chain?

answers.text: A food web contains fewer species than a single chain, so there is less that can go wrong when one is lost
Most organisms in a web have several food sources, so predators can shift to other prey if one is lost
A food web has no producers at its base, so it does not depend on the Sun for its energy supply
Energy is not lost as heat in a web, because organisms feed at several levels and reuse it

questions.text: A persistent pesticide is present at a very low level in the algae of a lake. In the food chain algae → small fish → large fish → osprey, where will the pesticide be MOST concentrated, and why?

answers.text: In the osprey, because it eats many contaminated fish and the toxin accumulates up the levels
In the algae, because that is where the pesticide enters and the base supports everything above
In the small fish, because they are the most numerous animals and absorb the toxin fastest
Equally across all four levels, because the toxin spreads evenly as organisms eat one another

questions.text: Sea otters are not very numerous, yet when they are removed from a kelp forest, sea urchins multiply and graze the kelp down to bare rock, and many other species disappear. This makes the sea otter a good example of a —

answers.text: producer, because it supports the kelp forest and the species that depend on the kelp
decomposer, because it recycles nutrients from dead urchins back into the water
primary consumer, because it feeds directly on kelp and so removes plant material
keystone species, because its effect on the community is far larger than its numbers suggest

questions.text: What is a trophic cascade?

answers.text: The steady loss of energy as heat at each trophic level, leaving less for each higher consumer
The buildup of a persistent toxin in the tissues of organisms as it moves up the food chain
A change at the top of a food web, such as losing a top predator, that ripples down through lower levels
The one-way flow of water from land to the ocean through a watershed during heavy rainfall

questions.text: After gray wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone in 1995, which sequence best describes the trophic cascade that followed?

answers.text: Wolves returned → elk numbers fell and elk avoided streambanks → willow and aspen recovered → beavers and songbirds increased
Wolves returned → elk numbers rose and elk crowded streambanks → willow and aspen declined → beavers and songbirds decreased
Wolves returned → willow and aspen died off → elk numbers rose → streambanks eroded and beavers declined
Wolves returned → elk numbers stayed constant → willow and aspen were unchanged → no other species responded

quizzes.title: Week 17 Reading Quiz: Biogeochemical cycles

questions.text: Which statement best describes how water moves through the water cycle?

answers.text: Water is used up by living things when they drink it and must be replaced by new water formed in the atmosphere
Water moves only from the land to the ocean and never returns to the land, so continents slowly lose their water
Water evaporates and is released by plants (transpiration), condenses into clouds, falls as precipitation, and returns as runoff or infiltration
Water falls as precipitation, then condenses into clouds, then evaporates from the ground, and finally returns to the oceans as runoff

questions.text: Which pair of processes moves carbon into and out of living things, forming the heart of the carbon cycle?

answers.text: Cellular respiration removes CO₂ from the air; photosynthesis returns CO₂ to the air
Photosynthesis removes CO₂ from the air; cellular respiration returns CO₂ to the air
Both photosynthesis and cellular respiration remove CO₂ from the air and store it in sugar
Neither process involves CO₂; carbon moves only through the decay of dead organisms

questions.text: Why does burning fossil fuels add carbon dioxide to the atmosphere so quickly?

answers.text: Burning fossil fuels creates brand-new carbon atoms that did not exist on Earth before, adding extra mass to the air
Fossil fuels are made mostly of pure oxygen, which is converted into carbon dioxide gas when it is heated
Burning fossil fuels speeds up photosynthesis, which releases CO₂ into the air much faster than usual
Fossil fuels hold carbon from ancient photosynthesis, and burning releases in a short time what took millions of years to store

questions.text: The air is about 78% nitrogen gas (N₂). Why can't plants and animals simply use this nitrogen to build their proteins and DNA?

answers.text: N₂ has a very strong triple bond that plants and animals cannot break, so bacteria must first fix it
The air contains very little nitrogen gas, so organisms must obtain all of their nitrogen from rocks
Nitrogen gas is poisonous to plants and animals, so they have evolved to avoid absorbing it
Plants absorb all the nitrogen gas before animals can reach it, leaving animals none for proteins

questions.text: A field of clover grows well without fertilizer, and its soil ends up richer in usable nitrogen. What is happening in the clover's roots?

answers.text: The clover's roots are absorbing nitrogen gas directly from the air spaces in the soil
The clover is making new nitrogen atoms by photosynthesis and releasing them into the soil
Denitrifying bacteria around the roots are converting soil nitrate into ammonium the clover can use
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the root nodules are converting N₂ gas into a usable form

questions.text: Decomposers break down a dead animal and release its nitrogen back into the soil as ammonium. What is this step of the nitrogen cycle called?

answers.text: Nitrogen fixation
Ammonification
Denitrification
Assimilation

questions.text: How does the phosphorus cycle differ from the carbon and nitrogen cycles?

answers.text: Phosphorus has no significant gas phase, so it cycles through rock, soil, water, and sediment
Phosphorus is the only one of the three with a major gas phase, so the atmosphere is its main reservoir
Phosphorus is not used by living things, so it cycles only through rock and never enters organisms
Phosphorus cycles faster than carbon and nitrogen because it moves quickly through the atmosphere

questions.text: In many ecosystems phosphorus is described as the "limiting nutrient." What does this mean?

answers.text: Phosphorus is toxic to most organisms, so its presence caps how many can survive there
Phosphorus blocks the amount of sunlight an ecosystem receives, which limits photosynthesis
Because phosphorus is often scarce, its shortage caps how much the ecosystem can grow
Phosphorus is so abundant that it is never in short supply, so other factors limit growth

questions.text: Fertilizer runoff triggers an algal bloom in a lake; soon after, the fish suffocate in a "dead zone." What directly causes the water to lose its oxygen?

answers.text: The living algae use up all the dissolved oxygen through respiration while they are blooming
Decomposers respire as they break down the mass of dead algae, using up the dissolved oxygen
The fertilizer reacts chemically with the dissolved oxygen and destroys it as soon as it enters
The extra nitrogen and phosphorus displace the dissolved oxygen by taking up space in the water

quizzes.title: Week 18 Reading Quiz: Populations & succession

questions.text: Two populations are graphed over time. Population X keeps rising ever more steeply and never levels off; population Y rises quickly and then flattens out. Which statement is correct?

answers.text: X shows exponential (J-shaped) growth and Y shows logistic (S-shaped) growth
X shows logistic (S-shaped) growth and Y shows exponential (J-shaped) growth
Both show exponential (J-shaped) growth because both rose quickly at first
Both show logistic (S-shaped) growth because both are limited by resources

questions.text: Which pair of factors adds individuals to a population?

answers.text: Deaths and emigration
Births and emigration
Deaths and immigration
Births and immigration

questions.text: A newly introduced population on an island grows exponentially for several months. Which condition best explains why exponential (J-shaped) growth is possible during this time?

answers.text: Predators, disease, and competition are strongly limiting growth and keeping the population in check
The population has already reached its carrying capacity and is now at its maximum size
Resources are effectively unlimited, and predation and competition are not yet limiting growth
Emigration is greater than immigration, so individuals are leaving faster than they arrive

questions.text: Which statement about carrying capacity (K) is most accurate?

answers.text: K is a fixed, permanent number that a population eventually reaches and then never drops below again
K is the maximum population size an environment can sustain, and it can shift as conditions change
K is the fastest rate at which a species can reproduce, and it stays the same for the species
K is the starting number of individuals in a population when it first enters a new area

questions.text: A sudden hard freeze kills roughly the same fraction of an insect population whether that population is crowded or sparse. This limiting factor is best classified as:

answers.text: Density-dependent, because weather conditions change as the population grows or shrinks
Density-dependent, because any factor that reduces population size depends on density
Density-independent, because its effect does not depend on how crowded the insects are
A biotic factor, because it acts on living organisms such as these insects

questions.text: In the classic lynx–snowshoe hare cycle, the hare population rises and then falls, and the lynx population follows the same pattern a step behind. Which best explains this rhythm?

answers.text: More hares support more lynx; more lynx reduce the hares; fewer hares starve the lynx, letting hares recover
The lynx and hares compete for the same plants, so whichever is more abundant crowds out the other
A density-independent factor such as winter weather rises and falls each year and controls both populations
The hares eat young lynx whenever the lynx become abundant, which drives the lynx numbers down

questions.text: What is the key difference between primary and secondary succession?

answers.text: Primary succession occurs in aquatic habitats such as ponds, while secondary succession occurs on dry land
Primary succession is fast because pioneer lichens spread quickly across the rock, while secondary succession takes much longer
Only secondary succession ends in a climax community, while primary succession stops at the pioneer stage
Primary succession starts on bare rock with no soil, while secondary succession starts where soil remains after a disturbance

questions.text: After a wildfire, a forest regrows within a few decades, but a new lava flow may take centuries to reach a mature forest. What best explains why the burned forest recovers so much faster?

answers.text: The fire added new nutrients to the ground, while the lava flow is completely lacking in nutrients
The burned site still has soil with nutrients, roots, and seeds, while lava must first build soil from rock
Lichens and mosses grow much faster on ash than on bare rock, which gives the burned forest a head start
Secondary succession skips the pioneer and climax stages, so the burned forest reaches maturity sooner

questions.text: Scientists cite three lines of evidence for a changing climate: the instrumental temperature record, the rising atmospheric CO₂ record with its fossil-fuel isotope fingerprint, and poleward/earlier shifts in species' ranges and timing. Why does drawing on three independent lines make the conclusion stronger than relying on any one alone?

answers.text: Because combining three measurements always makes the result exactly three times as accurate as any single measurement taken alone
Because biological evidence from living species is the only kind that truly counts, so the other two lines are redundant and unnecessary
Because using more lines of data automatically removes all uncertainty about the rate and the magnitude of change in the climate
Because independent lines from different fields converging on one conclusion are much harder to explain away than any single measurement

quizzes.title: Week 19 Reading Quiz: Biodiversity & human impact

questions.text: A biologist studies the range of different alleles for disease resistance carried by individuals within a single wild rabbit population. Which level of biodiversity is she measuring?

answers.text: Species diversity
Genetic diversity
Ecosystem diversity
Trophic diversity

questions.text: Why does an ecosystem with high species diversity tend to be more stable and resilient than one with very few species?

answers.text: More species means less competition for food and space, so populations rarely lose any members
Diverse ecosystems have fewer predators, so no prey population ever crashes in them
Many species create redundancy in the food web, so if one is lost, others can fill its role
More species means the ecosystem uses less energy overall, which leaves a bigger reserve

questions.text: Which of the following is the single largest cause of biodiversity loss worldwide?

answers.text: Habitat destruction and habitat fragmentation
Volcanic eruptions and large earthquakes
The normal aging of individual organisms
Seasonal changes in temperature and rainfall

questions.text: A non-native plant is introduced to Florida but causes no ecological or economic harm and simply blends into the landscape. Based on the scientific definition, is it "invasive"?

answers.text: Yes — any species that is non-native to an area is automatically considered invasive there
Yes — all introduced plants count as invasive, though introduced animals are judged differently
No — plants can never be classified as invasive, since only animals are able to spread
No — an invasive species must be both non-native and cause ecological or economic harm

questions.text: The Burmese python and the lionfish both spread explosively in their new Florida-area habitats. What best explains why invaders like these can multiply so successfully?

answers.text: They arrive without the predators, parasites, and competitors that limited them at home, and natives lack defenses
They reproduce more slowly than native species, so each one invests more care in its offspring and survives much longer
They are physically larger than every native species, so natives cannot compete or escape them
Florida's climate is too harsh for them, which forces them to reproduce faster to avoid dying out

questions.text: Which pairing of a Florida invasive species with the way it harms native communities is correct?

answers.text: Lionfish — grows into dense stands that crowd out native plants by shading them
Brazilian pepper tree — poisons the predators that try to eat it with a toxin in its skin
Cane toad — devours native reef fish with the venomous spines along its back
Burmese python — acts as an unchecked apex predator, eating native mammals in the Everglades

questions.text: Which list contains only renewable resources?

answers.text: Coal, oil, natural gas, and other fossil fuels
Oil, natural gas, most metal ores, and mineral deposits
Solar energy, wind, and a sustainably managed forest
Coal, wind, and most mineral deposits in the ground

questions.text: A fishery is usually called a "renewable" resource, yet many fisheries have collapsed from overfishing. How is this possible?

answers.text: Fisheries are actually nonrenewable resources, so they were mislabeled before collapsing
Renewable resources last only if harvested no faster than they can replenish themselves
Fish stop reproducing whenever humans are present, so no new fish replace those harvested
Overfishing converts the fish population into a mineral resource, which is nonrenewable

questions.text: If habitat destruction is the single largest cause of biodiversity loss, which conservation strategy most directly addresses that leading cause?

answers.text: Establishing protected areas and reserves that directly guard habitat
Breeding single endangered species one at a time in zoos and wildlife centers
Removing all predators from an ecosystem so prey populations can grow
Introducing more non-native species into a habitat to increase its diversity

quizzes.title: Week 20 Reading Quiz: Silent Spring & synthesis

questions.text: DDT washes into a lake at a very low concentration, yet fish-eating birds such as ospreys end up with by far the highest concentration in their bodies. Why?

answers.text: The ospreys drink far more of the contaminated lake water than any other animal, so they absorb the most DDT
DDT is chemically attracted to feathers and bone, so only birds absorb it from the lake and nothing else in the food web does
The birds spray DDT directly onto their nests while preening, which concentrates it in their bodies
A persistent toxin is not lost between levels but concentrates upward, so the top predator accumulates the toxin of everything below

questions.text: DDT did not usually kill adult raptors outright, yet their populations still crashed. What was the main reason?

answers.text: DDT built up as fat that made the adult birds too heavy to fly, so they starved before they could breed
DDT interfered with calcium in the females' eggshells, making shells so thin that few chicks hatched
DDT discolored the birds' feathers, making them so conspicuous that predators killed many adults
The adults stopped eating fish because DDT dulled their sense of smell and hunting ability

questions.text: Bald eagle, osprey, and peregrine falcon populations recovered in the decades after most uses of DDT were banned in the United States in 1972. What does this recovery best support?

answers.text: Raptors are naturally immune to pesticides, so some unrelated factor must have caused the decline
Eggshell thinning was never connected to DDT, so the recovery must have been a coincidence
DDT was a major contributor to the earlier declines, because removing it was followed by recovery
Raptors rapidly evolved thicker eggshells within a few years of the ban, so selection explains it

questions.text: A coastal wetland filters pollutants out of water and buffers a town from storm surge. These benefits are best classified as which category of ecosystem service?

answers.text: Regulating services
Provisioning services
Cultural services
Supporting services

questions.text: Nutrient cycling and soil formation are called supporting services rather than provisioning or cultural services. Why?

answers.text: Because they are the physical goods that people harvest from nature and carry home to use
Because they provide recreation, beauty, and spiritual value to the people who visit nature
Because they are the slow, underlying processes that make the other services possible
Because they occur only in the ocean, where nutrients cycle and sediments build up slowly

questions.text: Which statement best defines sustainability?

answers.text: Using as many natural resources as quickly as possible to maximize the present economy's growth
Meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own
Leaving nature completely untouched, harvesting nothing so that no resources are ever used
Replacing all natural ecosystems with managed farmland so that production is guaranteed forever

questions.text: Biology supports the view that humans are both members and shapers of ecosystems. Which pair of statements best captures this dual role?

answers.text: We are heterotrophs whose carbon cycles like any organism's (member); we can alter food webs and the climate (shaper)
We stand entirely outside the food webs of nature (member); and we have no effect on climate or ecosystems (shaper)
We are producers that make our own food (member); and we never change our surroundings (shaper)
We are immune to biomagnification (member); and we only ever restore ecosystems, never harm them (shaper)

questions.text: Follow one carbon atom. It leaves the air as carbon dioxide, becomes part of a sugar in a leaf, is eaten by an animal, and later returns to the air. Which sequence of processes does it pass through?

answers.text: Cellular respiration builds it into sugar in the leaf, then photosynthesis in the animal releases it to the air
Photosynthesis builds it directly into DNA, then digestion in the animal releases it to the air as CO₂
It stays locked in the sugar when eaten, is stored as animal fat, and never returns to the air
Photosynthesis builds it into sugar, then cellular respiration breaks the sugar down and releases it to the air

questions.text: The same molecule, DNA, ties together three units of the course. Which statement correctly matches DNA's role in genetics, evolution, and classification?

answers.text: DNA carries usable energy for cells (genetics); stores fat that natural selection acts on (evolution); and builds the walls that sort species (classification)
DNA is important only in genetics (heredity); it plays no role in evolution, and it is not used to sort organisms in classification
DNA is copied and inherited (genetics); its mutations supply variation for selection (evolution); its sequences reveal relatedness (classification)
DNA is made by ribosomes in genetics, by chloroplasts in evolution, and by mitochondria in classification, each in different cells
